title: Monic quadratic equations

findings.finding: No opening review rehearses common-factor factorisation or rearranging an equation to obtain zero on one side.
findings.breakdown: Both examples require taking out a variable factor, and p4-example-x also requires subtracting 36x from both sides. These prior skills are used without preparatory review.
findings.checked: All supplied teaching was checked. p3-identify already rehearses solving the resulting linear factors, so that piece has been removed from the candidate. It does not rehearse factorising an expanded expression or rearranging an equation.
findings.assumptions: Factorisation and equation operations are prior learning from the separately listed course booklets. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p3-null-factor-law, add: ‘Factorise: (a) x²+5x; (b) y²−8y; (c) 3x²−12x. Subtract the term on the right from both sides and simplify: (d) x²=4x; (e) 2y²=6y.’ Expected answers: x(x+5), y(y−8), 3x(x−4), x²−4x=0, 2y²−6y=0. These five short items fit within a one-page review.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses common-factor factorisation and obtaining zero on one side before the worked examples.

findings.finding: The complete unscaffolded solve task x²+4x=0 appears twice without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copy repeats the same equation and required response without changing the support or mathematical decisions.
findings.checked: Both whole tasks were compared, including their group instructions. Neither supplies intermediate working, additional parts, diagrams or an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.assumptions: The supplied order is the teaching order.
findings.doneWhen: One copy remains, or an explicit instructional purpose is supplied for retaining both.

findings.finding: A prediction and comparison run could expose why multiplying an equation by a nonzero constant preserves its solutions.
findings.breakdown: Existing questions include scalar multiples with the same roots, but do not ask students to predict or explain that relationship.
findings.checked: For any nonzero k, kx(x−3)=0 has precisely the roots 0 and 3. The proposed run uses common-factor factorisation and the null factor law already available here. Existing questions can supply most of the run without adding duplicate solve tasks.
findings.assumptions: Solutions are real numbers; no calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: After the routine common-factor practice, assemble a comparison using x²−3x=0 and existing p5-q3-a, p5-q3-d and p5-q3-e: x²−3x=0; 2x²−6x=0; 6x²−18x=0; −5x²+15x=0. Ask: ‘Before solving, predict which equations have the same solutions. Solve to check, then explain.’ Only the nonzero numerical multiplier varies; x(x−3) stays fixed. All have roots 0 and 3. Follow with existing p5-q3-i, 3x²+12x=0, whose roots are 0 and −4. Move the existing items into this run rather than copying them.

findings.doneWhen: Students predict, verify and explain the unchanged roots, then solve the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: Students could generalise when two common-factor quadratics have the same solutions.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the symbolic second-root formula in p7-q8 to a comparison of two equations.
findings.checked: For nonzero real a, b, c and d, the respective solution sets are {0, −b/a} and {0, −d/c}. They coincide exactly when b/a=d/c. Factorisation and the required symbolic root formula are available by p7-q8.
findings.assumptions: The coefficients are nonzero real numbers.

repair.proposal: After p7-q8-b, offer: ‘For nonzero real a, b, c and d, when do ax²+bx=0 and cx²+dx=0 have exactly the same solutions? Explain using their factors and give an example.’ Expected answer: b/a=d/c, since the roots are 0 and −b/a, and 0 and −d/c. Example: x²−3x=0 and −2x²+6x=0 both have roots 0 and 3.

findings.doneWhen: Students state and justify the condition and provide a valid example.

findings.finding: The introductory trinomial examples require PSF factorisation, but no opening review rehearses selecting signed factor pairs and constructing the binomial factors.
findings.breakdown: Step 2 presents completed factors. Students unable to recall the product-and-sum decision cannot reconstruct that central step.
findings.checked: All teaching and the preceding topic's supplied practice were checked. They rehearse common-factor factorisation and solving supplied factors, but not PSF factorisation of monic trinomials. The preceding topic supplies no review of this skill.
findings.assumptions: PSF factorisation is prior learning from Expand and Factorise Monic Quadratics. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p8-information, add: ‘Factorise using PSF. Write the required product, sum and chosen pair first: (a) x²+5x+6; (b) x²+x−6; (c) x²−7x+12.’ Expected answers: (a) product 6, sum 5, pair 2 and 3, factors (x+2)(x+3); (b) product −6, sum 1, pair 3 and −2, factors (x+3)(x−2); (c) product 12, sum −7, pair −3 and −4, factors (x−3)(x−4). These three items fit within a one-page review.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse signed product-and-sum selection and binomial construction before the examples.

findings.finding: The complete solve task x²−12x+20=0 appears twice without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both copies require identical mathematical decisions and responses.
findings.checked: The complete tasks and group instructions were compared. There are no differing givens, scaffolds, parts or diagrams, and no explicit purpose for repetition. Removing p10-q3-d would interrupt the coefficient variations in p10-q3-a–d and its relationship with p10-q3-i, so the earlier isolated copy is the smaller removal.
findings.assumptions: The supplied order is the teaching order.

repair.proposal: Remove p9-q2-l and retain p10-q3-d within its existing variation group.

findings.doneWhen: One unchanged solve task remains and the p10-q3 variation group is preserved.

findings.finding: Students could generalise how two integer roots determine a monic quadratic and when its roots coincide.
findings.breakdown: The task connects factor constants with roots of the opposite sign and generalises the repeated-factor structure already encountered.
findings.checked: Expanding (x−r)(x−s) gives x²−(r+s)x+rs. Its only possible roots are r and s, so it has one distinct solution exactly when r=s. Repeated factors occur in p3-identify, p8-guided-d and p10-q4; binomial expansion belongs to the listed prior factorisation content.
findings.assumptions: r and s are integers, with equality allowed; solutions are real numbers.

repair.proposal: After p10-q4-root, offer: ‘A monic quadratic has integer solutions r and s. Write its factorised equation and expand it to find its linear coefficient and constant. When does it have only one distinct solution? Construct an equation whose only solution is x=−5.’ Expected answer: (x−r)(x−s)=0, hence x²−(r+s)x+rs=0. One distinct solution occurs when r=s, giving x²−2rx+r²=0. For x=−5 only, (x+5)²=0 or x²+10x+25=0.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the coefficient relationships and correctly construct and explain a repeated-root equation.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already learned to clear variable denominators in equations, including two different binomial denominators such as x−2 and x+4? The separate Equations with Algebraic Fractions booklet establishes that the course covers this method, but its place before this booklet is unknown. The answer determines whether these tasks use prior knowledge or require additional teaching.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing factor order leaves the solution set unchanged.
A squared binomial is two identical factors and gives one distinct solution.
protectedGroups.varies: Square notation versus explicit repeated factors.

protectedGroups.observation: The zero of each linear factor depends on its sign and constant.
protectedGroups.varies: One factor at a time changes sign or constant.
protectedGroups.invariant: A product of two monic linear factors equals zero.

protectedGroups.observation: Rearrangement and common-factor solving remain applicable as coefficients and signs change.
protectedGroups.varies: One coefficient or its sign between neighbours.
protectedGroups.invariant: A square term equals a linear term.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing only the linear coefficient's sign changes the signed factor pair and reverses both roots.
protectedGroups.varies: The linear coefficient changes from 2 to -2.
protectedGroups.invariant: The leading coefficient, constant -3, table format and solution method.

protectedGroups.observation: Opposite linear coefficients with the same square constant produce opposite repeated roots.
protectedGroups.varies: The linear coefficient changes from -18 to 18.
protectedGroups.invariant: The constant 81, leading coefficient and repeated-factor structure.

protectedGroups.observation: A fixed product can correspond to different factor pairs, and the sum's sign determines the signs of those pairs.
protectedGroups.invariant: The constant 20, monic form, zero RHS and solving method.

protectedGroups.observation: With the same constant after rearrangement, a different linear coefficient selects a different factor pair.
protectedGroups.varies: The linear coefficient changes from 9 to 21.
protectedGroups.invariant: The equation form x²+bx=-20 and the rearrangement required.
